# Introduction

This report generates the results reported in our paper (but not the figures---see the script `final_paper_figures.R` for those).


```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 5,
                      fig.height = 3,
                      out.width = "75%",
                      message = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center")
options(list(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE))
theme_set( theme_classic() )

source( here::here( "empirical/load_and_prep_empirical_results.R" ) )



```

# Some statistics on the studies

Our count of studies is the following:
```{r}
whole_studies <- studies %>%
  group_by( Project,Collection, blocked ) %>%
  summarise( n = n() )
table( whole_studies$Collection, whole_studies$blocked ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

Our count of outcomes is the following:

```{r}
table( studies$Collection, studies$blocked ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```


Some statistics about the blocked studies across the `r nrow(filter( studies, blocked=="Blocked"))` outcomes they entail:
```{r}
studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked" ) %>%
  pivot_longer( c( n, ncv, nbar, J, Jcv, K, cluster_ICC, block_ICC, R2.1, R2.2, p.tx, R_ate, R_se ),
                names_to="statistic", values_to="value" ) %>%
  group_by( statistic ) %>%
  summarise( mean = mean(value),
             median = median( value ),
             sd = sd(value),
             min = min( value ),
             Q10 = quantile(value, 0.1),
             Q90 = quantile(value, 0.9),
             max = max( value ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

```


**The 10th and 90th percentile number of individuals, clusters and blocks are around: 850 to 17,500 (individuals), 30 to 495 (clusters), and 5 to 85 (blocks).**

```{r}
blocked = filter( studies, blocked =="Blocked" )

n = quantile( blocked$n, c(0.1, 0.9) )
J = quantile( blocked$J, c(0.1, 0.9) )
K = quantile( blocked$K, c(0.1, 0.9) )
bind_rows( n=n, J=J, K=K, .id = "unit" ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```





## Which studies have singletons and doubletons?

This table lists the number of singletons and doubletons for the Blocked experiments
```{r}
studies %>% 
  dplyr::filter( blocked == "Blocked" ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, num_singletons, num_doubletons ) %>% 
  knitr::kable(  )
```

We can tally the outcomes by study type.
Many of the studies had at least one singleton:
```{r}
studies %>% 
  group_by( blocked, Collection ) %>%
  summarise( n_outcome = n(),
             n_no_singletons = sum( num_singletons == 0 ),
             n_no_doubletons = sum( num_doubletons == 0 ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```



## Studies with low degrees of freedom

In this report, we define "Low" to be strictly less than 10 degrees of freedom, with degrees of freedom defined as
$$ df_{cons} =  J - 2K - 1 $$
Here are all studies with 30 or fewer "conservative" degrees of freedom (so low and near low):


```{r}
studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", cons_df <= 30 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( UniqueID, cons_df, n, J, K, Jbar, Jcv, ncov.1, ncov.2 ) %>%
  arrange( cons_df ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

# Some statistics on our estimators

For each outcome we calculate a bunch of ATE estimates and SE estimates.
We then look at the range of ATE estimates and the ratio of the max to min SE estimate.

We can then tally the number of outcomes with a large ranges of SE (2x or more) and/or ATE (0.10 or more):

```{r}
studies %>% 
  filter( blocked == "Blocked" ) %>%
  group_by( big_ate, big_se ) %>%
  summarise( n = n() ) %>%
  mutate( big_ate = ifelse( big_ate == "", "No", "Yes" ),
          big_se = ifelse( big_se == "", "No", "Yes" )
          ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```


## How often the ATE range is large

Here we count the number of ranges greater than 0.10 and 0.05:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( group, measure ) %>%
  filter( str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_10 = sum( Range >= 0.10 ),
             big_10 = n_10 / n,
             n_05 = sum( Range >= 0.05 ),
             big_5 = n_05 / n ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```

## How often estimated Standard error ratio is large

The `n_1.2`, etc are the number of outcomes with a ratio of that amount or larger.  The "big" is just the percent of outcomes.

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( group, measure ) %>%
  filter( !str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
              n_1.2 = sum( Range >= 1.2 ),
             big_1.2 = n_1.2 / n,
            n_1.5 = sum( Range >= 1.5 ),
             big_1.5 = n_1.5 / n,
             n_2 = sum( Range >= 2 ),
             big_2 = n_2 / n,
             max = max( Range ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```

## Stability connected to df

Here we divide our outcomes by low vs high degree of freedom, and then count how many ratios are large vs. small within those subgroups:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( low_df, group, measure ) %>%
  filter( !str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_1.2 = sum( Range >= 1.2 ),
             big_1.2 = n_1.2 / n,
             n_1.5 = sum( Range >= 1.5 ),
             big_1.5 = n_1.5 / n,
             n_2 = sum( Range >= 2 ),
             big_2 = n_2 / n ) %>%
  arrange( group, measure, desc(low_df) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```


We can also make a quick boxplot to show the difference in ratio by low vs high df:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  filter( measure == "ate" | measure == "se" ) %>%
  ggplot( aes( low_df, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ measure, scales="free" ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "Ratio/Range under different specifications" )

ggsave( file="range_boxplot.pdf", width = 5, height = 2 )
```

And singleton vs not:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  filter( measure == "ate" | measure == "se" ) %>%
  ggplot( aes( has_single, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ measure, scales="free" ) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs( title = "Ratio/Range for studies with and without singletons" )

```




## When are SE estimators defined?

In the paper we write: _While this model-free approach is appealing in theory, in practice this means design-based standard errors can only be estimated if every block X experimental arm has at least two or more clusters. Only three studies in our sample meet this condition; consequently, the design-based standard errors do not exist for XX out of 50 outcomes when the fully-interacted model (for individual or aggregate data) is implemented. The same limitation applies to heteroskedastic robust standard errors. For most outcomes, there are only 13 estimated standard errors, rather than 19 (See Supplemental Excel Spreadsheet 1)._

To motivate this, the following table counts the number of undefined estimators within each group given the set of covariates included.

```{r}
#cc <- combined %>%
#  dplyr::select( UniqueID, Covariates, Estimator, ATE_hat_std, SE_hat_std )
#skimr::skim( cc )
combined %>%
  group_by( Covariates, Estimator ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_ATE = sum( is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ),
             n_SE = sum( is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from=Covariates, values_from=c(n_ATE, n_SE) ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

This table counts the number of estimates for each outcome that are undefined (the different columns correspond to adjusting for all covariates, a single best covariate, or no covariates):

```{r}
combined %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, Covariates ) %>%
  summarise( #n = n(),
             n_ATE = sum( is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ),
             n_SE = sum( is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from=Covariates, values_from=c(n_ATE, n_SE) ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

## What is the average range and ratio?

The following table shows the average range (for ATEs) and average ratio (for estimated SEs) across all our outcomes:

This tells us, for example, that "On average, the largest standard error is around 33% larger than the smallest, across studies."
This is for the "best" covariate adjustment:

```{r}
ranges %>%
  dplyr::filter( Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  dplyr::filter( !str_detect( measure, "noFI" ) ) %>%
  group_by( group, Estimand, measure ) %>%
  summarise( avg = mean( Range ),

```


## ATE range and SE ratios vs study characteristics

We can see if  our "conservative df" for each study  predicts the range across estimators and the ratio of SE estimates (all studies with 30 df or more have been topcoded at 30 to make the plots easier to read):

```{r}
ranges %>%
  filter( group=="all" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) %>%
ggplot( aes(cons_df_adj, Range ) ) +
  #facet_grid(  measure ~ has_single, scales="free" ) +
  facet_wrap(  ~ measure, scales="free" ) +
  geom_jitter( aes( col=has_single  ), height=0, width=0.5 ) +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) +
  geom_smooth( aes( col=has_single  ), method="lm", se=FALSE)
```

Commentary: This plot does show there is some tendency for ranges and ratios to go down as DF goes up, but there is a lot of variation around that tendency.


We next look at the distribution of range/ratio of estimates across outcome, grouping by singleton status.  We see the studies with singletons tend to have smaller ATE ranges, and the range of SE estimates is marginally higher---note that the singleton studies SE ratios are over fewer estimators (none of the FI estimators are defined), which would generally push the ratios _lower_ as there are fewer points to take the max and min from.


```{r, fig.height=2}
ranges %>%
  filter( group=="all" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) %>%
ggplot( aes(has_single, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ measure, scales="free_x" ) +
  geom_boxplot()  +
  coord_flip()
```

Commentary: I am not sure if these plots are useful or informative.
I am not sure what they mean, either.

# Variation in the ATE Estimates

## Studies with a high range (more than 0.15) of ATE estimates

```{r}
ss <- studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", R_ate > 0.15 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Project, UniqueID, K, J, n, cons_df, R_ate, R_ate_Clu, R_ate_Per )

ss %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```


## Range within Estimand

If we go within study, we get the following average reduction across outcomes within estimand:
```{r}
  ssf %>% 
    mutate( rat = Ratio.x / Ratio.y ) %>%
    group_by( Estimand ) %>%
    summarise( mean_rat = mean( rat ),
               sd_rat = sd( rat ) ) %>%
    knitr::kable( digits=2 )
```


Still a threshold of 0.15.

```{r}
ss <- studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", R_ate > 0.15 | R_ate_Clu > 0.10 | R_ate_Per > 0.10 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Project, UniqueID, K, J, n, cons_df, R_ate, R_ate_Clu, R_ate_Per )

ss %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

Some statistics on the selected studies:
```{r}
cc <- combined %>%
  dplyr::filter( UniqueID %in% ss$UniqueID, Covariates == "best" ) 

cc %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, num_singletons, ncv, Jcv ) %>% 
  summarise( ATE_min = min( ATE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             ATE_max = max( ATE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             range = ATE_max - ATE_min,
             SE_avg = mean( SE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             n_est = n(),
             n_def = sum( !is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  arrange( UniqueID ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```


```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, out.width= "100%" }

ggplot( cc, aes(Estimator, ATE_hat_std, color = Estimand ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ UniqueID, scales="free_x", nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point( data=filter(cc,str_detect( Estimator, "MLM" ) ), 
              color="black", shape = 21, size = 3 ) +
  coord_flip() +
    theme(panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines"))
```

Note: The MLM estimators are circled to indicate they are not unbiased for either estimand, in principle.


Extending the overall plots from above, we can look at what study characteristics drive larger or smaller ranges, within estimand:

```{r}
rr <- rangesW %>%
  filter( Covariates =="best", group=="estimand" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) 

rr %>%
ggplot( aes(cons_df_adj, Range, col=has_single ) ) +
  facet_wrap( . ~ Estimand,  nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE) +
  labs( title = 'Range of ATE estimates within estimand' )
```

Range does go up as expected with average SE increasing:
```{r}
rr %>%
ggplot( aes(SE_avg, Range, color=has_single ) ) +
  facet_wrap( . ~ Estimand,  nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)

```


We can see if range depends on variation in block or cluster size:
```{r}
rr2 <- rangesW %>%
  filter( Covariates =="best", group=="all" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) 

ggplot( rr2, aes(Jcv, Range ) ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)

ggplot( rr2, aes(ncv, Range ) ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE)
```


We can use trees to predict what predicts larger range:

```{r}
source( here::here( "analysis/Simulation_Write_Up/create_analysis_tree.R" ) )
tree1<-create_analysis_tree(rr2,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "ncv", "Jcv", "SE_avg", "R2.1", "R2.2", "has_single", "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )
```

If we drop the average SE we get this:
```{r}
tree1<-create_analysis_tree(rr2,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "ncv", "Jcv", "R2.1", "R2.2",
                                                "has_single", "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )
```

These trees shows that uncertainty drives larger differences, and also that greater variation in cluster size drives larger differences, especially if there is variation in the cluster means.

If we look within estimand (i.e., fit our tree to the full set of 50 person ranges and 50 cluster ranges), we see that our datasets with larger R2.1 and no singletons have larger ranges (assuming the SEs are generally large):

```{r}
tree2<-create_analysis_tree(rr,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "Estimand", "ncv", "Jcv",
                                                "SE_avg", "R2.1", "R2.2", "has_single",
                                                "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )

```

## Comparing low DF to high DF studies

We can look to see if studies with high or low df have generally larger ranges:

```{r}
ra <- rr2 %>%
  group_by( low_df ) %>%
  summarise( avg_rng = mean( Range ),
             sd_rng = sd( Range ),
             Q05 = quantile( Range, 0.05 ),
             Q95 = quantile( Range, 0.95 ),
             n = n() )
ra$ratio = ra$avg_rng / min( ra$avg_rng )

ra %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

The low df studies tend to have higher ranges than the high df studies.

## How often are the SE estimates defined?

Here we look at 'best' and see how often the SE estimates are defined for each outcome.
We see that for 34 outcomes, 57% of our estimators are defined and for 16 outcomes all of them are defined.

```{r}
cc <- combined %>%
  filter( Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, Covariates ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_def = sum( !is.na( SE_hat_std ) ),
             per_def = n_def / n, .groups = "drop" )

table( cc$Covariates, cc$per_def )

```

## How much do SE ratios go down within Estimand?

In the following we look at how much the SE ratios shrink going within estimand.

```{r echo=FALSE}
 # Looking at how range decreases as we go within estimand
source( here::here( "empirical/calculate_all_ranges.R" ) )
  ss <- summary_stats_estimand %>%
    filter(Covariates == "best") %>%
    dplyr::select( UniqueID, Estimand, Ratio ) 
  ss
  ss1 <- summary_stats %>%
    filter(Covariates == "best") %>%
    dplyr::select(UniqueID, Range, Ratio)
  ssf <- left_join(ss, ss1, by = 'UniqueID')
  
  knitr::kable( ssf, digits = 2 )
  ggplot( ssf, aes( Ratio.y, Ratio.x ) ) +
    facet_wrap( ~ Estimand ) +
    geom_point() +
    coord_fixed() +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = 'red') +
    labs( x = "Overall ratio", y = "Within Estimand Ratio" )
```

This is the average reduction across outcomes:
```{r}
  ssf %>% 
    mutate( rat = Ratio.x / Ratio.y ) %>%
    group_by( Estimand ) %>%
    summarise( mean_rat = mean( rat ),
               sd_rat = sd( rat ) ) %>%
    knitr::kable( digits=2 )
```


# Are SEs for cluster weight smaller than individual?

We fit a multilevel model to our raw estimated standard errors, having a random intercept for the outcome and for the estimator.
We also allow for a "random slope" for estimand within outcome, as it is possible that some studies are better at targeting person vs cluster average effects.
We finally allow a random slope for studies with singletons, to see if some estimators have estimated SEs that change more depending on whether there are singletons present:

```{r}
library( lme4 )

combined$Covariates = factor( combined$Covariates,
                              levels = c( "best", "none", "all" ) )
M = lmer( log( SE_hat_std ) ~ Estimand + Covariates + has_single + I(log(1+cons_df)) + I(log(nbar)) + I(log(J)) + (1+has_single|Estimator) + (1+Estimand|UniqueID),
          data=combined )
arm::display(M)
```

We see no evidence that targeting person estimands is different from cluster estimands in terms of precision.
There is some variation in average uncertainty by estimator.

We can look at the exponentiated coefficients to see the multiplicative effect on the SE:
```{r}
exp( fixef( M ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

Relative to 'best', not controlling for anything means estimated SEs are 18% larger.  Controlling for everything makes them 10% smaller.
Bigger studies in terms of either n or J have smaller SEs, as expected.
The estimated SEs for the studies with singletons are generally smaller; it is unclear what that is coming from.


We can dig into which estimators are better or worse:

```{r}
ranef(M)$Estimator %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var="estimator" ) %>%
  rename( avg = `(Intercept)`,
          singletons = has_singlesingetons ) %>%
  mutate( avg = exp(avg),
          singletons = exp( singletons ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```

The estimators have no variation in the average estimated SE, but do differ when faced with studies with singletons.
In particular, MLM-FIcw is 6% larger, and LRicw-FE-crve is 12% smaller---the latter is likely due to poorly estimated CRVEs when there are singletons.



## Which estimators tend to be most extreme?

Here we tag when each estimator is either the 1st or second smallest or 1st or second largest SE estimate of all availables for that outcome (within the "best" covariate set).

```{r}
extreme <- combined %>%
  filter( Covariates == "best", !is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) %>%
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  mutate( ratio = max( SE_hat_std ) / min(SE_hat_std ),
          extreme = rank( SE_hat_std, ties.method = "first" ) <= 2 |
          rank( SE_hat_std, ties.method = "first" ) >= n() - 1 ) %>%
  filter( ratio > 1.25 ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by( Estimator, Estimand ) %>%
  summarise( n_def = n(),
             n_extreme = sum( extreme ),
             per = n_extreme / n_def )

extreme %>%
  arrange( per ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )


```

The `n_def` column is the number of outcomes where the estimator was even defined.

I'm not sure this table is particularly informative, but it does show that some estimators are more likely to be extreme than others.  The problem is some estimators aren't even defined, which robs them of the opportunity to be informative.
